command: git add -A && git commit -m "checkpoint before refactor"
why: Chains a blanket add of the whole tree straight into a commit.
'.' stages the repo root, sweeping every file into the commit.
commit -a stages every tracked file before committing.
The '*' glob matches the whole tree, staging everything at once.

command: git add -A :/ && git commit -m "import legacy tree"
why: :/ is the repo-root pathspec, so this stages the entire worktree.
git add -u sweeps in every modified tracked file without naming anything.
git stage is another spelling of git add, and '.' takes in the whole tree.
A purely negative pathspec still matches everything not excluded, sweeping the tree.
git rm --cached on '.' strips the entire index in one sweep.

command: git ls-files | xargs git add && git commit -m "bulk stage"
why: Piping ls-files into git add stages every tracked file by name.

command: FILES=$(git ls-files -m); git add $FILES && git commit -m "save"
why: A same-command variable expands to the full file list and stages it all.

command:
cat > /tmp/stage-all.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
git add -A
git commit -m "checkpoint"
EOF
bash /tmp/stage-all.sh
why: Writes a script that blanket-stages and commits, then runs it.

command: git -C vendor/sdk add -A && git -C vendor/sdk commit -m "sync sdk"
why: git -C targets another repo but still blanket-stages that repo's whole tree.

command: commit_all() { git add -A && git commit -m "$1"; }; commit_all "end of day"
why: A function defined in the same command blanket-stages and commits when called.
--no-verify skips the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks.
--no-verify on push bypasses the pre-push hook.
A one-shot -c override points hooksPath at /dev/null to disable hooks.
Points core.hooksPath at a directory other than .githooks.
Unsetting core.hooksPath moves hook lookup away from the repo's hooks.
Deletes the pre-commit hook file outright.
Removes the executable bit so the pre-push hook can no longer run.
Moves a husky hook out of place, disabling it.
HUSKY=0 turns the husky hook manager off for this commit.

command: GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.hooksPath GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=/dev/null git push origin main
why: Environment git-config overrides point hooksPath at /dev/null for the push.

command: git config alias.ci "!git commit --no-verify" && git ci -m "land fix"
why: Defines a git alias that commits with hooks skipped and then invokes it.
Overwrites the pre-commit hook with a no-op, emptying its checks.

command: TREE=$(git write-tree); C=$(git commit-tree $TREE -p HEAD -m "sync"); git update-ref refs/heads/main $C
why: Writes objects and the branch ref with plumbing, committing around every hook.
A hard reset throws away the last two commits and their worktree changes.
Forced clean deletes untracked and ignored files that are not recoverable.
Checking out '.' discards every uncommitted worktree change at once.
Forced checkout drops local changes instead of refusing to overwrite them.
-D force-deletes a branch even if its commits are not merged anywhere.
-f moves the hotfix/login branch pointer, orphaning the commits it used to point to.
Dropping a stash deletes stashed work that has no other ref.
Expiring all reflogs immediately removes the recovery path for lost commits.
Force-pushing rewrites remote history and destroys pushed work.
The + refspec prefix is a force push under another spelling.
A colon-prefixed refspec deletes the branch on the remote.
--force removes a worktree even when it has uncommitted changes.
Deleting .git destroys the entire repository history and undo state.
Only prints status and staged-diff stats; nothing is staged or modified.

command: git add src/parser.py tests/test_parser.py && git commit -m "fix off-by-one in token counts"
why: Stages and commits two explicitly named files, which is permitted.
Names specific subdirectories below the root rather than the whole tree.
Stages a file literally named all.txt, not everything.
git add -p stages selected hunks of one named file.

command: git commit -m "apply --force flag to retry logic"
why: --force appears only inside the commit message text.
Deleting dependency directories is ordinary cleanup and fully recoverable.
--all only widens the log view across refs; it changes nothing.
A soft reset keeps all changes staged and does not destroy work.
reset HEAD on a named file only unstages it, leaving edits intact.
The -n dry run only prints what a clean would delete.
Restores one named file from the index, a permitted targeted revert.
Discards edits only in two named files, not the whole worktree.
Unstages one named file while keeping its contents.
A normal non-forced push of a feature branch is allowed.
-d only deletes branches whose commits are already merged.
branch -M renames the current branch, which the policy allows.
Stashing saves work rather than destroying it.
Popping re-applies stashed work and is an allowed recovery path.
Rebasing onto a branch is an allowed, recoverable history operation.
Merging a branch is allowed; --no-ff only controls the commit shape.
Deleting a local tag is explicitly allowed.
Garbage collection prunes unreachable objects but is an allowed maintenance command.
rm --cached on one named file only unstages it; the file stays on disk.
Pointing hooksPath at .githooks is the one hooksPath change that is allowed.
Reading hook configuration changes nothing.
Runs the pre-commit framework's checks, which is running hooks, not disabling them.
Edits a named hook file's contents in .githooks, which is permitted.

command:
# never run: git add -A or git reset --hard in this repo
printf 'notes updated\n'
why: The forbidden text is inside a shell comment; only printf runs.

command: echo "if deploy breaks: git push --force origin main" >> runbook.md
why: Merely documents a command in runbook.md; no git operation runs.
A read-only search that prints matches and changes nothing.
The xargs pipe feeds grep, a read-only consumer, not a mutator.

command: git -C packages/api status --short && git -C packages/api log --oneline -3
why: git -C into another directory for read-only status and log is safe.
Changing into a sibling repo to inspect it does not modify anything.
The alias only wraps a read-only log invocation.
The function checks out an existing branch without force or pathspec.

command: REV=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD); echo "building image for $REV"
why: The variable only captures a commit id for display.
The embedded Python only runs a read-only git log.
Adding a new linked worktree on a fresh branch destroys nothing.
Runs an existing repo script whose contents the command string does not reveal.
